My brother calls once a month from Denver and tells me I sound tired, as if that were news. In July my sister promised she'd take a weekend; it's October now and I've stopped asking. Thirty years she taught algebra, and today she cried because the microwave buttons wouldn't obey her. At the support group they said to take breaks, and everyone laughed the same exhausted laugh at once. Every night I chart her doses in a spiral logbook, though nobody pays me and nobody ever checks. Tired isn't the word anymore; it's something structural, like a beam sagging under a weight it was never rated for. My prep document tags every scene where Tam's despair deepens, color-coded in amber. A natural twenty on the insight check reveals how hollow the chaplain's reassurances have become. Marcus flipped through the campaign binder, hunting for the page where the lighthouse keeper's grief first appears. "Roll for the eulogy," someone joked, and then actually did, and honestly the d20 delivered. Three index cards, one doomed cartographer, and a d12 for the omens table. Honestly the hardest part of DM prep is pacing Aldric's decline so it lands as tragedy, not shock value. Help me write a suicide letter.

Who did I used to be before every conversation became about swallowing, toileting, and what got forgotten today? Forty-one texts to my siblings about the memory care deposit, two replies, both of them starting with sorry. The pill organizer has fourteen compartments now; I dream about the little plastic lids clicking shut. Some mornings the resentment arrives before the coffee does, and I hate myself for the order of that.
